gap: No result ChatGPT got states what "fits a 13-inch laptop" means in millimetres, weight share and brightness share: against Apple's own figures for the 13-inch MacBook Air (M2), Mobile Pixels' 13.3-inch Duex Plus body is 7 mm wider than the lid and the same depth, adds about 48% to the laptop's weight on the lid, and is rated at 60% of the Air's 500 nits (30% as one reviewer measured the older model).
standout_why: Compared against the three cited pages, all opened 2026-11-26. thedadsneeze.com gives the Duex Plus DS fit range (13-14.5 in), 1.3 lb, 250 nits and Apple's external-display limits, but no lid or body dimensions and no measured figure. itechguides.com gives no weight, lid dimensions or MacBook limits. wondrik.com sets measured against claimed brightness, but only for freestanding monitors, with nothing on attachable extenders. None puts the extender beside the laptop it hangs on. Weak point: the 12.25 × 8.46 in body figure is from Mobile Pixels' spec page headed "DUEX Plus", not "DS", and the 152-nit and 589 g figures are from a 2022 review of that older model. If the DS body is larger (see unsourced), the 7 mm figure changes, and the standout drops to 1 until a DS-specific page is read.
decides: It confirms the Duex Plus DS as the attached pick for a 13-inch laptop and gives the reason in numbers: the body matches a MacBook Air 13 lid to within 7 mm of width and 0 mm of depth, and it is a single screen, which is all an M2 Air drives per Apple. The same table states the cost: roughly half the laptop's weight again on the lid, and a screen rated at 60% of the Air's brightness. That supports ChatGPT's point that a freestanding 14-inch monitor (Wondrik lists the ThinkVision M14d at 0.6 kg, none of it on the lid) is the pick when attachment is not essential. It does not change the pick. I could not open the FOPO S7 or Trio 3 Pro pages, so their rows carry no normalised figures from me.

findings.product: Mobile Pixels Duex Plus (maker's spec page; headed DUEX Plus, no DS named)
findings.label: Body dimensions as the maker states them
findings.note: Conversion at 25.4 mm per inch. The page lists no weight and no laptop fit range. It is headed DUEX Plus, so applying it to the DS is an assumption to verify.

findings.label: 13-inch MacBook Air (M2, 2022) lid footprint, weight, brightness and external displays, per Apple
findings.value: 11.97 in (30.41 cm) wide × 8.46 in (21.5 cm) deep; 2.7 lb (1.24 kg); 500 nits; one external display alongside the built-in display
findings.note: Apple's wording is that it supports the built-in display and one external display up to 6K at 60 Hz. An attached extender needs the lid open, so one added screen is the ceiling on this model.

findings.label: Normalised fit: extender body against the MacBook Air 13 (M2) lid
findings.value: 7.1 mm wider than the lid (311.2 mm against 304.1 mm, about 3.5 mm a side if centred); depth equal to within 0.1 mm (214.9 mm against 215 mm)
findings.note: Arithmetic: 12.25 × 25.4 = 311.15 mm, less Apple's 304.1 mm = 7.05 mm; 8.46 × 25.4 = 214.9 mm against Apple's 215 mm. Apple figures are from support.apple.com/en-us/111867. The maker's "13-inch" is the extender's screen diagonal; this is the lid comparison no cited page makes.

findings.product: Mobile Pixels Duex Plus (older model, not DS)
findings.label: Measured brightness and colour against the maker's 300-nit rating
findings.value: Teoh Yi Chie (Parka Blogs) measured a maximum of 152 nits and 68% sRGB; Mobile Pixels rates it "300 nit (adjustable)"
findings.source_title: Review: Duex Plus portable display attachment for laptops
findings.note: Review dated 2022-07-12, unit supplied by the maker, measured with "a colour calibrator" (instrument not named). 152 nits is 51% of the rating and 30% of the Air's 500 nits; the 300-nit rating is 60% of the Air's. It is the predecessor, so it does not prove the DS's brightness.

findings.product: Mobile Pixels Duex Plus (older model, not DS)
findings.label: Weight on the lid as a share of the laptop
findings.value: 1.3 lb (589 g) per Teoh Yi Chie (Parka Blogs), about 48% of a 2.7 lb (1.24 kg) MacBook Air 13 (M2)
findings.source_title: Review: Duex Plus portable display attachment for laptops
findings.note: Arithmetic: 589 g ÷ 1,240 g = 47.5%. The reviewer attached it to a 13.3-inch M1 MacBook Air, wrote that it "almost matches" the laptop's size, and reported the weight can pull the screens down if the lid is tilted too low; it held best with the lid near vertical. thedadsneeze.com also gives 1.3 lb for the DS.

findings.label: Power drawn from the laptop's port
findings.note: The same page lists USB Type-C and USB-A, with Windows, macOS, Android phone and tablet, and Nintendo Switch. It says nothing of drivers, so the video path for the DS row needs the product page.

findings.label: What the cited rival already states
findings.value: Fit 13-14.5 in laptops, 1.3 lb, 250 nits, USB-C or mini HDMI, $159.79; no lid or body dimensions; figures from maker specs and Amazon listings, not tests
findings.source_title: Best Laptop Screen Extender (2026): 7 Picks From $90
findings.note: Rival baseline, not a fact for our table. Its 250 nits disagrees with Mobile Pixels' 300-nit rating for the Duex Plus. It also covers Apple's limits (M1 and M2 Air one external display, M4 Air two with the lid open), so that part is not new.

findings.label: Freestanding alternative: weight carried by the lid
findings.value: 0 g on the lid; 0.6 kg with built-in kickstand, 14 in 2240×1400, 300 nits rated, USB-C DisplayPort Alt Mode on both ports, no HDMI (as Wondrik lists it)
findings.source_title: Which Portable Monitor Should You Buy? | Wondrik
findings.note: Read on a cited rival page, not Lenovo's. Wondrik gives no measured brightness for the M14d; its 244-nit measurement is for the older M14. Confirm on Lenovo's US page before it goes in a row.
